title: E-Safety: Smart, Safe and Secure Online

pages.c16-p01: Explain the difference between an active and a passive digital footprint and describe how your online reputation can affect your future
pages.c16-p02: Describe what data companies collect and why, and explain how cookies, app permissions and location sharing affect your privacy
pages.c16-p03: Critically analyse information on social media, explain the difference between misinformation and disinformation, and use lateral reading to check a source
pages.c16-p04: Explain how generative AI can create realistic deepfakes and edited images that are hard to tell apart from authentic content, and how they can be used to mislead and influence people
pages.c16-p05: Recognise scams and fraud aimed at young people, including phishing texts, fake giveaways, money mule offers and account-recovery scams, and know how to report them
pages.c16-p06: Explain how strong passwords, two-factor authentication and encryption (including HTTPS) keep accounts and communication secure, and how to recover a hacked account
pages.c16-p07: Describe how loot boxes, virtual currencies and other in-game spending features work, and explain why some are compared to gambling
pages.c16-p08: Critically analyse how social media is designed to hold attention, and describe how comparison culture, influencers and advertising rules affect wellbeing
pages.c16-p09: Explain why consent matters when sharing images, describe what sextortion is and how to respond, and know how to get an image removed
pages.c16-p10: Describe, in simple terms, the legal and ethical implications of online behaviour, including the Computer Misuse Act 1990, communications offences and data protection law, and know where to get help in Northern Ireland

q.q: Which of these is an example of an active digital footprint?
o: The cookies a shopping site stored on your laptop
A record of which adverts you scrolled past
A review you wrote of a local restaurant
The location data your phone logs in the background
q.why: An active footprint is content you deliberately choose to post.

q.q: Which of these is an example of a passive digital footprint?
o: A bio you wrote on your gaming profile
A photo you uploaded to your public story
Your search history being stored by a search engine
A comment you left on a YouTube video
q.why: Passive data is collected about you without you deliberately sharing it.

q.q: What is meant by your online reputation?
o: The privacy settings you have chosen on each account
What people think of you from what they can find online
The list of websites you have visited this year
The number of followers you have on all your apps
q.why: Reputation is the impression others form from your online presence.

q.q: A friend posts a party photo of you without asking. Which statement is correct?
o: It only affects your friend's footprint
It becomes part of your digital footprint too
It cannot be seen by employers because you did not post it
It is automatically deleted after 24 hours
q.why: Content others post and tag you in is linked to you.

q.q: Why is deleting an old post not a guarantee that it has gone?
o: Deleted posts are moved to a public archive by law
Apps are not allowed to delete posts
It may already have been screenshotted or shared
Deleting a post only hides it from you
q.why: Copies made by others are outside your control.

q.q: Cara deletes a rude comment, removes a tag from a party photo and posts a video of her football training. What is she mainly doing?
o: Reducing her targeted advertising
Creating a passive digital footprint
Building a more positive digital footprint
Turning on two-factor authentication
q.why: She is removing negatives and adding positives that others will see.

q.q: Which is the best reason to search your own name online?
o: To see what others such as employers might find
To increase how many people visit your profile
To turn off cookies on every website
To delete other people's accounts with your name
q.why: It shows you the footprint other people will see.

q.q: Which setting stops photos you are tagged in from appearing on your profile until you agree?
o: Location services
Tag approval
Two-factor authentication
Autoplay
q.why: Tag approval lets you accept or reject tags first.

q.q: A pupil says: 'My passive footprint doesn't matter because I never post anything.' What is wrong with this?
o: Data is still collected from searches, apps and location
Passive footprints are only created by tagging
Passive footprints only exist for adults
Not posting deletes your passive footprint
q.why: Passive data builds up even if you never post.

q.q: Which test from Year 8 helps you decide whether to post something?
o: SIFT: Stop, Investigate, Find, Trace
STOP: Save, Tell, Off, Phone
CIA: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability
THINK: True, Helpful, Inspiring, Necessary, Kind
q.why: THINK is the posting checklist; SIFT is for checking sources.

q.q: What is a cookie?
o: An advert that appears when you open an app
A small text file a website stores on your device
A program that scans your computer for viruses
A type of encrypted message sent between phones
q.why: Cookies remember information such as logins and settings.

q.q: Which cookie is most likely to be used to follow you across many websites?
o: A third-party advertising cookie
An essential login cookie
A shopping basket cookie
A preference cookie for dark mode
q.why: Third-party cookies are set by advertisers to track you across sites.

q.q: Why do websites in the UK show cookie banners?
o: To prove to visitors that the website uses HTTPS
The law says they must check whether you are over 18
The law says they need consent for non-essential cookies
To install anti-malware software on your device first
q.why: Consent is needed for non-essential cookies.

q.q: Which is the best location setting for a weather app?
o: Approximate location, only while using the app
Precise location, always
Share location with all contacts
Precise location, only when the phone is locked
q.why: A weather app only needs a rough idea of where you are, when you use it.

q.q: What is targeted advertising?
o: Showing the same advert to everyone on a website
Adverts that must be approved by parents
Adverts shown only on television
Choosing adverts for each person using data about them
q.why: Profiles built from your data decide which adverts you see.

q.q: What could the hidden metadata in a photo reveal?
o: The password of the phone that took it
The GPS location where it was taken
The apps installed on the phone
The names of everyone who liked it
q.why: Metadata can include date, time and location.

q.q: A free torch app asks to read your contacts. What is the best response?
o: Allow it, then delete your contacts later
Deny it, because torches use too much battery
Allow it, because free apps need data to work
Deny it, because a torch does not need contacts
q.why: Only grant permissions an app genuinely needs.

q.q: Under UK GDPR, what is a subject access request?
o: Asking a website to stop showing adverts
Asking an app for permission to use your camera
Asking the police to investigate a scam
Asking an organisation for a copy of your data
q.why: It is your right of access to the personal data held about you.

q.q: In the UK, from what age can you normally agree to an online service using your data without a parent's consent?
q.why: The UK age of digital consent is 13.

q.q: Why is allowing an app to read your contacts a privacy issue for other people?
o: It sends them adverts by post
It changes their privacy settings
It deletes their numbers from your phone
It shares their details without them agreeing
q.why: Your contacts' personal data is shared without their consent.

q.q: What does the phrase 'if you are not paying for the product, you are the product' mean?
o: Free apps cannot collect any personal data
Users of free apps must pay later
Free apps are always lower quality than paid apps
Free apps make money from data about their users
q.why: Your data is used to sell advertising.

q.q: A fake account deliberately invents a story about a politician to influence voters. This is:
o: Clickbait
Misinformation
Disinformation
Lateral reading
q.why: Deliberately false information is disinformation.

q.q: Your grandad shares a false news story because he believes it is true. This is:
o: Malinformation
Disinformation
Misinformation
A deepfake
q.why: False but shared in good faith is misinformation.

q.q: Posting someone's real home address to cause them harm is an example of:
o: Malinformation
Disinformation
Clickbait
Misinformation
q.why: Malinformation is true information shared to cause harm.

q.q: What do fact-checkers do when they read laterally?
o: Open new tabs to see what others say about a source
Check whether the page has a professional design
Read the whole page carefully from top to bottom
Count the number of adverts on the page
q.why: Lateral reading means checking independent sources.

q.q: Why can a professional-looking website still be unreliable?
o: Professional sites are not allowed to be checked
Search engines only list unreliable sites
Professional sites never use HTTPS
Anyone can make a site that looks professional
q.why: Appearance is easy to fake, so check who is behind it.

q.q: What does SIFT stand for?
o: Search, Inspect the page, Filter the results, Tell
Stop, Ignore the source, Forward it, Trust it
Share, Investigate the author, Follow them, Tag
Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace
q.why: SIFT is a four-step method for checking information.

q.q: Which tool would best show that a 'breaking news' photo is actually years old?
o: An authenticator app
A screen time report
A cookie banner
A reverse image search
q.why: It finds earlier copies of the same image.

q.q: Why does a blue tick not prove an account is trustworthy?
o: Blue ticks are only given to scammers
Blue ticks are only for news companies
Blue ticks expire after one day
On some platforms anyone can pay for a tick
q.why: Verification badges can be bought on some platforms.

q.q: What is an echo chamber?
o: A space where you mostly see views you already agree with
A website that repeats adverts
A chat where messages are deleted after reading
A group call with a sound delay
q.why: False ideas are rarely challenged inside an echo chamber.

q.q: A post says all Fermanagh schools are closed tomorrow but has no link. What is the best first check?
o: Check whether it uses capital letters
Look at the school's own app or website
Count how many people have shared it
Share it and ask if anyone knows
q.why: Official sources are the best place to confirm.

q.q: What is generative AI?
o: A filter that changes the colour of photos
AI that only sorts emails into folders
Software that removes viruses from computers
AI that creates new text, images, audio or video
q.why: Generative AI produces new content from learned patterns.

q.q: Which describes a deepfake?
o: AI media of a real person doing something they never did
A real photo with the brightness and colours turned up
A cartoon avatar designed to look like your own face
A real video with automatic subtitles added to it
q.why: Deepfakes fake a real person's face, body or voice.

q.q: Why is it becoming harder to spot AI-generated content?
o: AI tools keep improving and make fewer obvious mistakes
Only experts are allowed to view the original AI images
Phones now remove the clues from AI content automatically
All AI content is now hidden inside normal photos
q.why: As AI improves, visual clues disappear, so check the source.

q.q: What is voice cloning?
o: Changing a recorded song into a different key
Using AI to copy a person's voice from a recording
Recording two people speaking at the same time
Sending the same voice note to many people at once
q.why: A short recording can be enough to clone a voice.

q.q: Which is the most reliable way to check a video of a footballer promoting an investment?
o: Check the video is high resolution
Check his official accounts and trusted news
See if the video has lots of likes
Watch whether his lips match the words
q.why: Checking the source is more reliable than looking for glitches.

q.q: Some families agree a secret safe word. What is this for?
o: Checking a caller is really family, not a cloned voice
Unlocking the family's shared streaming account
Logging new devices into the home Wi-Fi network
Turning parental controls on and off on a console
q.why: A safe word defeats voice-cloning scams.

q.q: Which of these is a harmful use of generative AI?
o: Giving a voice to someone who has lost theirs
A clearly labelled illustration for a news story
Special effects in a film
A fake image of a politician to influence voters
q.why: Using AI to mislead and influence behaviour is harmful.

q.q: Which statement about AI-generated sexual images of under-18s is correct?
o: They are only illegal if they are shared
They are illegal even though they are fake
They are legal because no real photo was taken
They are legal if made as a joke
q.why: The law covers fake and AI-made images to protect young people.

q.q: Which clue might suggest an image is AI-generated?
o: The image is in colour
The photo was taken outdoors
The person is smiling
Jumbled text in the background
q.why: AI often struggles with text, hands and fine details.

q.q: When you use AI to make an image for a project, what is good practice?
o: Remove all credits from the image
Present it as a real photograph
Use a classmate's face without asking
Label it as AI-generated
q.why: Labelling stops people being misled.

q.q: A 'friend' asks you to forward a code that just arrived by text. What is most likely happening?
o: The app is giving you a reward
Your phone needs a software update
Someone is trying to log in to your account
Your friend has changed phone networks
q.why: The code proves who is logging in; sharing it gives away your account.

q.q: What is a money mule?
o: Someone who buys and sells second-hand phones online
Someone who lets criminals move money through their account
A program that secretly steals people's bank details
A person employed to carry cash between bank branches
q.why: Moving criminal money is money laundering.

q.q: What is the maximum prison sentence for money laundering in the UK?
o: 2 years
14 years
5 years
6 months
q.why: Money laundering is very serious and can carry up to 14 years.

q.q: Where should you forward a phishing email in the UK?
o: report@phishing.gov.uk
The sender's address
Your friends, to warn them
q.why: Phishing emails go to report@phishing.gov.uk; texts go to 7726.

q.q: Why do 'free game currency generator' sites ask for your password?
o: To add the currency to your account
To prove the site is legal
To check your age
To steal your account
q.why: No legitimate site needs your password to give you items.

q.q: Which payment method is the biggest red flag when buying concert tickets on social media?
o: A card payment through an official ticket site
Buying through the band's official website
A bank transfer to a stranger
Paying at the venue box office
q.why: Bank transfers to strangers offer little protection.

q.q: Conor is offered £100 to let someone pay £800 into his account and send £700 on. What is this?
o: An account-recovery request
A loot box
A legitimate part-time job
Money mule recruitment
q.why: Letting criminals use your account is money laundering.

q.q: What does the number 7726 spell on a phone keypad?
o: STOP
SCAM
SAFE
SPAM
q.why: 7-7-2-6 spells SPAM.

q.q: Which feeling do scammers most often use to rush you?
o: Calm, such as 'take your time'
Urgency, such as 'claim within 1 hour'
Confusion, such as 'read the terms'
Boredom, such as 'nothing to see here'
q.why: Urgency stops you checking.

q.q: You have entered your card details on a fake site. What should happen first?
o: Wait to see if any money is taken
Tell a parent and contact the bank immediately
Post about it to warn your followers
Delete the browser history
q.why: The bank can block the card quickly.

q.q: What does HTTPS do?
o: Stores your passwords safely so you don't forget them
Checks that a website is run by an honest company
Blocks all adverts and pop-ups on a website you visit
Encrypts data travelling between your browser and a website
q.why: HTTPS secures the connection, not the honesty of the site.

q.q: A phishing site shows a padlock. What does this mean?
o: The site is run by the government or a large bank
The connection is encrypted, but the site can still be fake
The site has been checked by experts and is safe to use
The site is not able to collect or store your password
q.why: Criminals can use HTTPS too, so check the address.

q.q: What is encryption?
o: Compressing data so that it downloads much faster
Deleting data automatically once it is no longer needed
Scrambling data so only the intended receiver can read it
Copying data to a backup drive in case it is lost
q.why: Encrypted data looks meaningless without the key.

q.q: What does end-to-end encryption in a messaging app mean?
o: Only the sender and receiver can read the messages
Messages disappear after they are read
Messages can only be sent on Wi-Fi
The company reads messages to keep users safe
q.why: Not even the app company can read them.

q.q: What is a data breach?
o: When you forget your password and have to reset it
When personal data such as passwords is stolen or leaked
When a website asks for your consent to use cookies
When a phone runs out of storage and deletes files
q.why: Breaches can expose millions of logins.

q.q: Why does reusing the same password on many sites increase risk?
o: One breach lets criminals into all your accounts
It makes the password shorter
It turns off encryption
Sites share passwords with each other
q.why: Criminals try stolen logins on other sites.

q.q: Which password is strongest and easiest to remember?
o: abcdefgh12345678
KettleFermanaghRocket
Enniskillen2010!
q.why: Three random words make a long password that is hard to crack.

q.q: Two-factor authentication combines something you know with:
o: Your username typed in twice to prove it is you
Something you have or are, such as your phone or fingerprint
A second, different password that you also know
A security question about the name of your first pet
q.why: The two factors must be different kinds.

q.q: Which type of 2FA is generally the hardest to phish?
o: A passkey or security key
A code sent by email
A memorable word
A code sent by text message
q.why: Passkeys are tied to your device and the real website.

q.q: Ryan's account is hacked but he can still log in. What should he do first?
o: Delete the hacked account straight away
Post an apology to his followers
Secure his email account
Change his profile picture
q.why: Email is used to reset everything else.

q.q: What are backup codes for?
o: Sharing your account with a friend
Turning off two-factor authentication
Getting into your account if you lose your phone
Logging in without a password every time
q.why: They are a safe way back in when your second factor is unavailable.

q.q: What is a loot box?
o: A free reward for logging in each day
A chest you open by solving a puzzle
A box that stores your saved games
A paid item that gives a random reward
q.why: You pay without knowing what you will get.

q.q: Gems cost £4.99 for 500. A skin costs 1,200 gems. How much real money must you spend?
q.why: You need 3 packs (1,200 ÷ 500 = 2.4, rounded up), and 3 × £4.99 = £14.97.

q.q: In the same example (3 packs of 500 gems, skin costs 1,200), how many gems are left over?
q.why: 1,500 − 1,200 = 300 gems left over.

q.q: Gems cost £2.99 for 300. An item costs 800 gems. How much must you spend?
Why do games often use virtual currency?
o: It makes spending feel less like real money
It stops players from spending too much money
The law forbids showing in-game prices in pounds
It makes every item cheaper than its real price
q.why: An extra step hides the real cost.

q.q: Which feature do loot boxes share with gambling?
o: Paying for a result decided by chance
Always paying out prizes in real money
Only being sold in shops, not online
Being illegal for people of all ages
q.why: Payment plus chance links them.

q.q: In the UK, how are loot boxes currently treated by law?
o: They are banned for everyone
They are not classed as gambling
They are only allowed in free games
They count as gambling and need a licence
q.why: UK law does not currently class them as gambling.

q.q: What did the games industry's 2023 principles say about under-18s?
o: They should not buy loot boxes without parental permission
They should be banned from all online games
They should be able to cash out loot box prizes
They should get loot boxes free of charge
q.why: Industry principles require parent or guardian permission.

q.q: What is pay-to-win?
o: Paying gives you an advantage over other players
Winning cash prizes for reaching top scores
Paying a fee to enter an online tournament
Earning money by streaming your games online
q.why: Money, not skill, gives the edge.

q.q: Why should you wait before buying a 'limited-time' offer?
o: Prices always drop by half after 24 hours
Limited-time items are illegal to buy at once
Time pressure creates FOMO and rushed spending
Waiting a day earns you free virtual currency
q.why: A pause lets you decide calmly.

q.q: What is persuasive design?
o: Designing adverts that use bright colours
Designing websites that are easy to read
Designing technology to change how people behave
Making apps work for people with disabilities
q.why: It is used to keep people on apps for longer.

q.q: Which feature removes any natural stopping point in a feed?
o: A log out button
Screen time limits
Infinite scroll
Do Not Disturb
q.why: There is always more content to see.

q.q: Why do streaks keep people opening an app every day?
o: Streaks are required by law
Streaks make the app load faster
They fear losing what they have built up
Streaks unlock real money
q.why: Losing a streak feels like a loss.

q.q: Why can likes on posts feel like a slot machine?
o: Most likes are given automatically by bots
The reward is unpredictable, so you keep checking
Likes can be swapped for cash once you have enough
Each like costs the sender a small amount of money
q.why: Unpredictable rewards are especially habit-forming.

q.q: Which UK body says influencer adverts must be obviously identifiable?
o: The Internet Watch Foundation
The Advertising Standards Authority
CEOP
The Information Commissioner's Office
q.why: The ASA, with the CMA, sets and enforces these rules.

q.q: An influencer is paid by a brand that controls the post. How should it be labelled?
o: #ad at the start
#collab at the end
#sp in the comments
No label for videos
q.why: Ads must be clearly labelled upfront.

q.q: Why is comparing yourself to influencers' posts often unfair?
o: Posts are edited highlights, not everyday life
Every post is checked by the government
Influencers are not allowed to use filters
Influencers only post their bad days
q.why: Feeds are highlight reels.

q.q: Which is a sign that screen time is harming someone?
o: They watch a film at the weekend
They video call a grandparent weekly
They regularly lose sleep scrolling at night
They use a laptop for homework
q.why: Lost sleep is a key warning sign.

q.q: Which action best breaks the 'trigger' stage of the attention loop?
o: Moving the app to your home screen
Keeping a streak going
Turning off non-essential notifications
Turning on autoplay
q.why: Fewer notifications means fewer triggers.

q.q: A post says '#gifted #collab, use my code for 10% off'. What is the best analysis?
o: It is fine because it mentions a discount
It is honest advice from a friend
It is advertising and should be clearly labelled #ad
It is not advertising because no money was paid
q.why: A discount code suggests commission, so it is commercial.

q.q: What does consent mean when sharing images?
o: Clear permission given freely, without pressure
Permission from anyone in the photo's group chat
Permission that cannot be changed later
Permission given after being asked many times
q.why: Consent must be free and can be withdrawn.

q.q: Which is true about nude images of under-18s in the UK?
o: They are only illegal if an adult took or asked for them
They are legal as long as both people agree to it
Taking, sharing or keeping them is illegal, even of yourself
They are legal if they are deleted within one day
q.why: The law protects anyone under 18.

q.q: What is sextortion?
o: Threatening to share an intimate image unless someone pays
Editing a photo with an app to remove the background
Selling your own photos to a stock image website
Sharing a photo of someone with the person's consent
q.why: It is a form of blackmail.

q.q: Someone threatens to share an image unless you pay. Why should you not pay?
o: Paying is illegal for under-18s
Paying deletes your evidence
Paying makes the police unable to help
Paying usually leads to more demands
q.why: Criminals often come back for more.

q.q: What should you do with the messages from someone attempting sextortion?
o: Forward them to friends for advice
Delete them so nobody sees
Screenshot them and keep them as evidence
Reply asking them to stop
q.why: Evidence helps police and platforms act.

q.q: Which organisations run Report Remove?
o: The Advertising Standards Authority and the CMA
The Information Commissioner's Office and CEOP
Childline and the Internet Watch Foundation
The PSNI and the Office of Communications
q.why: Report Remove is a Childline and IWF service.

q.q: Who can use Report Remove?
o: Only people with a police reference
Anyone under 18 in the UK
Only people who live in England
Only adults over 21
q.why: It is for under-18s across the UK.

q.q: You are sent a nude photo of a classmate. What should you do?
o: Save it on your phone to show the police later
Don't forward or save it, and tell a trusted adult
Ask the whole group chat who sent it first
Forward it to a teacher yourself so they can see it
q.why: Forwarding or saving causes harm and is illegal.

q.q: Sextortion criminals often pretend to be:
o: A teacher from your school
A police officer
A bank manager
A young person of a similar age
q.why: Fake profiles of similar-aged young people build trust quickly.

q.q: Logging into a friend's account with a password you saw them type breaks which law?
o: Online Safety Act 2023
Data Protection Act 2018
Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
Computer Misuse Act 1990
q.why: Knowing a password is not permission to use it.

q.q: Which Northern Ireland law covers sending grossly offensive messages to cause distress?
o: Malicious Communications (NI) Order 1988
Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
Computer Misuse Act 1990
Data Protection Act 2018
q.why: It covers indecent or grossly offensive messages meant to cause distress or anxiety.

q.q: What is the main aim of the Online Safety Act 2023?
o: To make platforms protect users, especially children
To ban all social media accounts for under-16s
To make every online message end-to-end encrypted
To give every home in the UK free internet access
q.why: Platforms have duties, regulated by Ofcom.

q.q: Who regulates online platforms under the Online Safety Act 2023?
o: CEOP
Ofcom
The ICO
The ASA
q.why: Ofcom is the regulator for online safety.

q.q: What is the age of criminal responsibility in Northern Ireland?
q.why: From 10, young people can be prosecuted in NI.

q.q: Which is Northern Ireland's 24-hour crisis helpline?
o: PSNI on 101
Lifeline on 0808 808 8000
Childline on 7726
Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040
q.why: Lifeline supports people in distress or despair.

q.q: Which is an example of something legal but unethical?
o: Sharing a friend's embarrassing photo without asking
Uploading a whole film without permission
Hacking into a teacher's email
Selling malware online
q.why: It may not be illegal, but it is unfair and hurtful.

q.q: You want to complain that a company misused your personal data. Who should you contact?
o: The Information Commissioner's Office
CEOP at the National Crime Agency
Ofcom, the communications regulator
The Advertising Standards Authority
q.why: The ICO enforces data protection law.

q.q: Dylan says his threatening messages were 'only a joke'. Which is correct?
o: It is legal if they are friends
It is only a crime if he is over 18
It is legal if the messages are deleted
A joke is not a defence for threatening messages
q.why: The effect and intent of the messages matter, not the excuse.
